chunks.text: All right. Good morning. I think we're on our live stream straight away, so we've got Bring It Up on the Public Finance Prohibition on Providing Public Funds to gangs Amendment Bill, and we've got the Maori Women's Welfare League presenting to us. So Hope is going to be joining us online.

Morena. Can you see me? We can, Hope. Yes. Great to have you, and we can hear you as well. We've got you down for 10 minutes. We've read your written submission, but feel free to leave some time at the end for questions as well. Okay. I won't really need 10 minutes, but thank you. Do I just start?

Yep. Fire away. Cool. Okay, thank you. Yeah, I think I'm your first person this morning. I just really wanted to reiterate what I've said in our written submission about many members of our organization have connections to people in gangs. And I just want to highlight to you the concern around the potential for the removal of access to funding for programs around rehabilitation Whatever that is.

I've sat in Waitangi Tribunal hearings and heard from organizations who are unable to get funding because of their associations with gangs by whakapapa. And I just want to point out to you that one of the concerns is the words, so Section 73A (1) , about the Crown must not pay money indirectly.

So this is where the concern about funding organizations who have got really good programs for, it might be for people in gangs who often have a history of trauma. And I want to also draw your attention to the Gangs Act because the definition includes an association with a gang.

If people have served their crime and are out of prison, it just feels like they're never going to actually leave that history, that they're never what they've in the pa- That's really all I wanted today, because I did in my written submission. Great. But I wanted to just raise to you the concerns that I have around the wording, both in the bill that's been proposed, as well as the connection to the Gangs Act.

So you're leaving it up to the public servants to try and differentiate who they give their funding to and not give their funding to. Great. Thank you, Hope. We've got a question from Dr Lawrence Sunam. Okay. Kia ora. Thank you, Chair. Thank you so much, Hope. Just looking at your submission where you talk about that, "We agree that public money should not be used to fund organized crime."

Can I just check with you then, have you given any thoughts on what an alternative could potentially look like? What would be your sort of ideal scenario? Well, I think you'll know more than I do who's actually been funded to provide programs and who's having success with programs for things like pastoral or trauma-led rehabilitative and healing programs.

So I think there should be a deliberate strategy for that investment rather than saying the government's not going to fund anything associated with the gangs. There has to be something available. Okay. And I'll see, Hope, if we've got questions from any other members.

Doesn't look like we do. So we're really grateful for you joining us this morning, Hope. Thank you for your oral submission and the written submission as well. Really appreciate your time, so thank you. Okay. Thank you. Okay, members, that was our only oral submission for this morning, so we just have or whether we wish to private checks.
